questions.stem: One who can speak two languages fluently.

options.option_text: Polyglot (one who speaks MANY languages — more than two)
Bilingual (correct: 'bi' = two; bilingual = fluent in two languages ✓)
Monolingual (one language only)
Multilingual (more than two languages)

questions.explanation: B is correct. BILINGUAL = fluent in two languages (bi=two + lingual=of language). Compare: monolingual (one), bilingual (two), trilingual (three), multilingual/polyglot (many). A polyglot typically speaks more than two.

questions.stem: A place where books are kept for reading or borrowing but not for sale.

options.option_text: Bookstore (place where books are sold)
Library (correct: a library is a place where books are kept for reading/borrowing, not selling ✓)
Archive (archives store historical documents/records, not primarily for public borrowing)
Repository (general storage — not specific to books)

questions.explanation: B is correct. LIBRARY = a place where books and other materials are kept for people to read or borrow, free or at low cost, not for sale. Bookstore/bookshop = books for sale. Archive = historical documents. This is one of the most basic one-word substitution questions.

questions.stem: A doctor who specialises in the care of children.

options.option_text: Podiatrist (foot specialist)
Gynaecologist (specialist in women's health)
Paediatrician (correct: paediatrics = branch of medicine dealing with children; paediatrician = child specialist ✓)
Geriatrician (specialist in elderly care)

questions.explanation: C is correct. PAEDIATRICIAN = a doctor specialising in children's health. Root: Greek paidos (child) + iatros (physician). Compare: geriatrician (elderly), cardiologist (heart), dermatologist (skin), neurologist (nervous system).

options.option_text: Claustrophobia (fear of enclosed spaces)
Acrophobia (correct: acro = heights; phobia = fear; acrophobia = fear of heights ✓)
Agoraphobia (fear of open/crowded places)
Hydrophobia (fear of water; also rabies)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ACROPHOBIA = irrational fear of heights (Greek: akros = at the top). Common phobia list: acrophobia (heights), claustrophobia (enclosed spaces), agoraphobia (open/public spaces), arachnophobia (spiders), hydrophobia (water), xenophobia (strangers/foreigners), nyctophobia (darkness).

questions.stem: One who does not believe in the existence of God.

options.option_text: Agnostic (one who believes God's existence cannot be known — not the same as disbelieving)
Atheist (correct: an atheist is one who disbelieves in God or gods ✓)
Theist (one who BELIEVES in the existence of God — opposite)
Deist (one who believes in a God who created but doesn't intervene)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ATHEIST = one who does not believe in God (a + theist; 'a' is Greek prefix meaning 'without'). Compare: theist (believes in personal God), deist (believes in creator God who doesn't intervene), agnostic (believes truth is unknowable). These distinctions are tested in SSC vocabulary sections.

questions.stem: A government run by a small group of people.

options.option_text: Democracy (government by the people)
Monarchy (government by a single ruler — king/queen)
Oligarchy (correct: oligarchy = government or power exercised by a small, elite group ✓)
Theocracy (government based on divine authority/religion)

questions.explanation: C is correct. OLIGARCHY = rule by a few (Greek: oligos = few + arkhein = to rule). Government types: democracy (demos = people), monarchy (monos = one), oligarchy (few), theocracy (theos = god), plutocracy (wealth), autocracy (single unlimited power), bureaucracy (bureau = office). These are heavily tested.

questions.stem: A person who looks on the bright side of things.

options.option_text: Pessimist (looks on the dark side — opposite)
Nihilist (believes nothing has meaning)
Optimist (correct: an optimist always expects the best outcome and sees positive aspects ✓)
Cynic (distrusts people's motives; sceptical)

questions.explanation: C is correct. OPTIMIST = a person who tends to see the best in things and expect favourable outcomes. Root: Latin optimus = best. Antonym: pessimist (expects worst). Related: optimism, optimistic. Easily confused with: cynic (not just negative — specifically distrusts human motives).

questions.stem: A person who pretends to be what he or she is not.

options.option_text: Sycophant (one who flatters to gain advantage)
Hypocrite (correct: a hypocrite claims to have virtues or beliefs they don't actually possess — pretends to be what they are not ✓)
Charlatan (one who falsely claims professional skills — close but more specific to skills/knowledge)
Renegade (one who deserts and betrays a group)

questions.explanation: B is correct. HYPOCRITE = a person who professes beliefs or virtues they do not actually possess; one who pretends to be what they are not. Charlatan is similar but specifically refers to false expertise. Sycophant = flatterer. Root: Greek hypokrits = actor on stage.

options.option_text: Patricide (killing of one's father)
Fratricide (correct: frater = brother (Latin); fratricide = killing of one's brother ✓)
Matricide (killing of one's mother)
Homicide (killing of a human being)

questions.explanation: B is correct. FRATRICIDE = killing of one's brother (Latin frater = brother + -cide = killing). Common -cide words: fratricide (brother), sororicide (sister), patricide (father), matricide (mother), infanticide (infant), regicide (king), genocide (ethnic group), homicide (human), suicide (self).

questions.stem: A person who is indifferent to pleasure and pain.

options.option_text: Hedonist (one who pursues pleasure — opposite)
Masochist (one who enjoys their own pain — different)
Stoic (correct: a stoic endures hardship without complaint, remaining indifferent to pleasure or pain ✓)
Ascetic (one who practises severe self-discipline, often for religious reasons — similar but not identical)

questions.explanation: C is correct. STOIC = a person who can endure pain or hardship without showing feelings; indifferent to pleasure and pain. From Stoicism, the ancient Greek philosophy founded by Zeno. An ascetic avoids pleasure for spiritual purposes, but a stoic is characterised by emotional indifference to both pain and pleasure.

questions.stem: A person who has just started learning a subject.

options.option_text: Expert (opposite — one with advanced skills)
Veteran (long-experienced person — opposite)
Novice (correct: a novice is a person new to a field or activity; a beginner ✓)
Prodigy (one with exceptional talent, usually young — not specifically about being new)

questions.explanation: C is correct. NOVICE = a person new to and inexperienced in a job or situation; a beginner. Synonyms: beginner, neophyte, tyro, rookie, apprentice. Root: Latin novus = new. A prodigy has exceptional talent (not necessarily a beginner); a neophyte is a close synonym to novice.

questions.stem: A group of fish swimming together.

options.option_text: Herd (correct group noun for cattle, elephants — not fish)
Flock (correct for birds, sheep — not fish)
Shoal (correct: a shoal or school of fish = a large group swimming together ✓)
Pack (wolves, dogs — not fish)

questions.explanation: C is correct. SHOAL (or SCHOOL) = a large group of fish swimming together. Collective nouns: shoal/school of fish, flock of birds, herd of cattle/elephants, pack of wolves, pride of lions, murder of crows, gaggle of geese, pod of whales/dolphins. These collective nouns are frequently tested.
